paper_title: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Lipman et al., 2023) is the dominant recipe for image and video generation (Esser et al., 2024; Black Forest Labs, 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; HaCohen et al., 2024; Z-Image Team et al., 2025; Black Forest Labs, 2025). Typically, diffusion transformer (DiT) (Peebles & Xie, 2023) generates in compressed latent space, and convolutional decoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014; Esser et al., 2021) maps the latents to pixels. The decoder complicates deployment and can add substantial inference cost. For example, on H100, generating 5-second video with 4-step Wan 1.3B model (Zheng et al., 2026b) takes 2.8 seconds for sampling and another 1.9 seconds for decoding, adding about 70% overhead. Recent work obtains much faster decoders with comparable quality (Zhu et al., 2026; Kang & Kwak, 2026; Li et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026), suggesting that the decoder is largely redundant. This raises the question: what is the minimal network architecture for producing final pixels from latent diffusion model? We show that simple linear head can replace the decoder while improving pixel quality. Our method, Decoding Without Decoder (DWD), finetunes pretrained latent DiT by adding linear output head (the DWD head) in parallel with the DiTs original output layer (the denoising head). The denoising head continues to drive denoising steps, then the DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step only. The dual-head separation distinguishes DWD from previous approaches, whose denoising output leads to final pixels: latent models decode it, pixel models output it directly. This couples pixel fidelity to denoising, causing tradeoff between detail rendering and denoiser learnability (Yao et al., 2025; Skorokhodov et al., 2025). DWD decouples the two roles: the DWD head is trained with pixel quality losses (Esser et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018), while the denoising head is anchored to the frozen pretrained model to preserve sample content. The separation is most evident on pixel diffusion models, where the denoising head already predicts the final output. These predictions smooth fine detail because they estimate conditional means under ℓ2 loss. Applying perceptual losses directly to them (Lin & Yang, 2023; Berrada Ifriqi et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026b) risks collapsing sample diversity, as our shared-head ablation fails to improve FID  (Table 1)  . In contrast, separate head improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43. We evaluate DWD across latent and pixel generators on ImageNet, text-to-image, and video generation  (Fig. 1)  . Removing the decoder improves nearly all FID metrics across tested latent image models. On Wan (Wang et al., 2025) video, warping error drops by 23%, with visibly less detail distortion and flickering. On text-to-image pixel diffusion, DWD recovers photorealistic textures. To summarize, we show that: latent DiT needs no decoder: finetuning its last few blocks with an additional linear head suffices, reducing inference cost, improving ImageNet FIDs, and lessening detail distortion and flickering in Wan video. The dual-head separation also improves pixel diffusion models, producing better texture detail in text-to-image generation and state-of-the-art ImageNet FID of 1.43 among pixel flow models.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Latent-space diffusion. VQGAN (Esser et al., 2021) trains autoencoders with reconstruction, perceptual (Zhang et al., 2018), and adversarial (Goodfellow et al., 2014) losses, and LDM (Rombach et al., 2022) uses this perceptual compression to reduce diffusion cost. VA-VAE (Yao et al., 2025), REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025), and RAE (Zheng et al., 2026a) address the gap between reconstruction quality and diffusability. DC-AE (Chen et al., 2025) and Qwen-Image-VAE-2.0 (Zhang et al., 2026) increase spatial compression while preserving reconstruction fidelity. SSDD (Vallaeys et al., 2025) and PiD (Lu et al., 2026) replace conventional decoders with distilled pixel diffusion models. PiD and LTX-Video (HaCohen et al., 2024) also stop latent sampling early, letting the decoder complete the remaining denoising. Zhang et al. (2024) improve latent generators by applying losses to images produced through the VAE decoder. These approaches retain standalone decoding network. DWD instead produces the final pixels through linear head on the existing DiT, reusing its last-layer tokens and computation without an extra decoder.

(b) DWD retains the denoising head for latent denoising and adds parallel DWD head that produces the final pixels only at the final step, bypassing this decoder. DWD finetunes the pretrained generators final blocks and heads (fire icon), while freezing all previous blocks (ice icon). Time and conditioning are omitted for clarity. Pixel-space diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion models denoise directly in pixel space without an autoencoder. They overcome difficulties in high-resolution generation through multiscale architectures and specialized output pathways (Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Crowson et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026a), or improved prediction targets (Li & He, 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Zirvi et al., 2026). AsymFlow (Chen et al., 2026a) and L2P (Chen et al., 2026d) finetune pretrained latent models to perform denoising in pixel space, altering the flow trajectory and sample content (see Appendix B.4 for comparison). In contrast, DWD preserves the original latent trajectory rather than converting the model to pixel diffusion. DWD finetuning is also more efficient, since only the last few transformer blocks and output heads are updated with shallow backpropagation, whereas latent-to-pixel conversion must backpropagate through the entire network to adapt to pixel-space inputs.

sections.title: 3 DECODING WITHOUT A DECODER
sections.content: A pretrained latent DiTs last-layer tokens already encode rich pixel information (Gan et al., 2025; Akarken et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c): least-squares linear projection recovers most of the image structure before any finetuning  (Fig. 3)  . DWD exploits this by appending linear head that produces final pixels directly from these tokens, bypassing the decoder at inference (Fig. 2(b)). Separating the pixel readout from the denoising output lets each be trained with its own objective: pixel quality losses for the DWD head, and trajectory anchoring to preserve denoising behavior. 3.1 PRELIMINARIES We describe latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022) using the flow matching convention (Lipman et al., 2023). pretrained autoencoder encodes an image or video into latent representation z0. The forward process mixes the latent z0 with Gaussian noise to form zt = (1 t)z0 + tϵ, where ϵ (0, I) and [0, 1] denotes diffusion time. flow model (zt, t, c) (cid:55) ˆu trains network with extra conditioning to estimate the conditional mean of velocity := ϵ z0, using an ℓ2 flow matching loss. At inference, the model uses this velocity to progressively transform Gaussian noise into denoised latent sample ˆz0, running from = 1 toward = 0 (Song et al., 2021; Liu, 2022; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023). Finally, the decoder maps ˆz0 to the final image or video x. For the models studied here, the denoising network is diffusion transformer (DiT) (Peebles & Xie, 2023; Esser et al., 2024), which processes tokenized noisy latent zt with multiple transformer blocks (Vaswani et al., 2017), and feeds the last-layer tokens (after normalization and modulation) to linear output head that produces patch-wise denoising prediction. This is the denoising head, shown in Fig. 2(a). 3.2 DWD HEAD Our goal is to produce final pixels from pretrained latent DiT without decoder, subject to two constraints: minimal additional computation, and preservation of the pretrained denoising trajectory.

The remaining reconstruction mismatch can be addressed by finetuning the DiT. This inspires us to adopt simple linear DWD head that maps each token to pixel patch: ˆxi = Linear(hi) = hi + b, (1) where and are learnable weights and bias, and ˆxi is the pixel patch corresponding to token hi. This design places the DWD head in parallel with the denoising head, both reading the same lastlayer tokens. The linear head is the minimal form of this separate pixel output, which can optionally be extended with lightweight convolutional refiner (Appendix A.1). The predicted patches are then assembled into the final image or video ˆx, with color space conversion where needed (Appendix A). Efficiency. By reusing the DiTs nonlinear computation, the linear head is lightweight readout with negligible cost for common pixel patch sizes. Pixel patch size follows the combined downsampling factor of the autoencoder and tokenizer. The most common spatial factor of 16 gives 16163 patch per token. For video models, an additional temporal factor of 4 expands each patch to four frames. For most tested models, the total number of output dimensions per token stays below the DiTs hidden dimension. Separating denoising and pixel outputs. DWD achieves trajectory preservation and pixel rendering through clear separation of outputs: the DWD head is trained with pixel quality losses, while the denoising head drives sampling and is anchored to the pretrained model (Sec. 3.3). This dual-head separation distinguishes our work from prior diffusion-based image and video generators, where the denoising output serves as bottleneck pathway to final pixels. Final-step pixel rendering. The DWD head is only used at the final denoiser evaluation step, where the DiT input is small but nonzero. The nonzero timestep is important: treating DiTDWD as latent decoder at t=0 substantially worsens quality (Sec. 4.1), while the t>0 noise gives the pixel head freedom to create detail that the denoised latent would have smoothed away. Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021) is not used in the final step since its role is to steer the trajectory, whereas our final step does not advance the trajectory. 3.3 FINETUNING We finetune the last transformer blocks (typically K=48 for large text-conditioned models, see Appendix for details), both output heads, and the last modulation, keeping the prefix frozen. sections.title: IMAGENET GENERATION
sections.content: We show that DWD consistently improves FID across both latent and pixel baselines. We then ablate the separate head design and show that fusing the two heads degrades quality despite the same training losses, and also study the effect of head capacity and final timestep. Setup. We test two latent models, SiT-XL/2-REPA (Ma et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025) with the SDVAE decoder (Rombach et al., 2022) and SiT-XL/2-REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025) with its end-to-end tuned E2E-VA-VAE decoder (Yao et al., 2025), and two pixel models, JiT-H/16 (Li & He, 2026) and AnisoFlow-H/16 (Zirvi et al., 2026). DWD extensions are finetuned on ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), with training schedules detailed in Appendix A.2. We report FID (Heusel et al., 2017) and Inception Score (IS) (Salimans et al., 2016) under the ADM evaluation protocol (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021). Improvement over latent diffusion baselines. Removing the decoder improves both latent baselines  (Table 1)  : FID improves from 1.38 to 1.36 for REPA and from 1.12 to 1.06 for REPA-E, with IS improving as well. The two baselines use different latent spaces and decoders, yet linear head improves on both. Removing the decoder also saves 622 decoder GFLOPs for REPA, 2.6 the cost of single denoiser evaluation, and 252 decoder GFLOPs for REPA-E.

Larger circles mark the defaults used in Table 1. (b) Qualitative results also confirm the trend: DWD at its default timestep recovers skin and fabric texture, while DWD at tfinal=0 is as smooth as the baseline. The large panels are zoomed crops, with the full image inset. Improvement over pixel diffusion baselines. The pixel models have no decoder to remove, so DWD only adds second output trained with pixel quality losses. As shown in Table 1, DWD improves JiT from 1.90 to 1.85 FID and AnisoFlow from 1.55 to 1.43, new state of the art among pixel flow models, while raising IS by 35 points. This also narrows the FID gap between pixel and latent models on ImageNet. Separate head vs. shared head. The pixel-model gains have two sources: the pixel quality losses, which latent decoders are trained with but pixel models normally lack, and the separate head that receives them. The w/o separate head rows in Table 1 isolate the latter by fusing the two heads in both training and inference, so the denoising head receives both pixel losses and trajectory anchoring at their respective timesteps, with everything else unchanged. This degrades baseline FID (1.55 to 1.71 for AnisoFlow), so the losses alone do not account for the gain. The degradation reflects conflict: the ℓ2 denoising loss favors mode coverage, whereas LPIPS and adversarial losses favor perceptual quality but collapse diversity (better IS but worse FID than the baseline). Trajectory anchoring cannot fully counteract this interference, so the pixel losses need separate head. Linear vs. convolutional head. We ablate the capacity of the linear DWD head by adding small convolutional residual refiner conditioned on the linear prediction and the last-layer tokens (DWDconv; Appendix A). This extension brings no consistent improvement across the ImageNet models in Table 1. linear head therefore suffices to obtain the quality gains under our tested settings. Nonzero final timestep. Fig. 4 sweeps the final timestep at which the DWD head is evaluated. Quality degrades toward t=0, where the input is the fully denoised state decoder would receive, and recovers at small positive timestep. This shows that the DWD head needs partially denoised input to produce high-quality pixels, rather than mimicking decoder applied to clean state. 4.2 TEXT-TO-IMAGE GENERATION We show that DWD replaces the decoder with matched quality on latent baselines, including fewstep distilled model, and recovers photorealistic texture detail on the pixel baseline. We also ablate the adversarial loss to show that it is not critical on text-to-image generation. Setup. We test two latent models built on FLUX.2 klein 9B (Black Forest Labs, 2025), the 32-step Base model and its distilled 4-step variant, and one pixel model, AnisoFlow-L/16-T2I (Zirvi et al., 2026) (0.9B). All DWD extensions are finetuned on public real-image datasets (Wang et al., 2026a; Desai et al., 2021; Schuhmann et al., 2022) at mixed aspect ratios. We evaluate at 10241024 on COCO-10k (Lin et al., 2014; 2024) (FID, patch FID (pFID) (Lin et al., 2024), HPSv3 (Ma et al., 2025), HPSv2.1 (Wu et al., 2023)), OneIG-Bench (Chang et al., 2025), and LongText-Bench (Wu et al., 2025). Training and sampling details are in Appendix A.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Decoder removal with reduced distortion and flickering. DWD removes the 0.28-PFLOP Wan decoder and replaces it with linear head at negligible cost  (Table 3)  , while also improving visual quality. The baseline decoder distorts fine detail such as small text and dense structures, and the distortion changes from frame to frame, which appears as flicker (Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 6). With the decoder removed, the linear DWD head keeps these details stable and legible, noticeably reducing flickering (see the project page for video comparisons). Warping error captures this artifact directly: it aligns consecutive frames by optical flow, masks occlusions, and measures the remaining photometric error, which DWD reduces by 23% (1.52 to 1.18) in Table 3. VBenchs temporal flickering score is less suitable here, since it is the raw pixel difference between consecutive frames without accounting for residual motion, and it saturates near its maximum for both models. The remaining VBench dimensions and HPS metrics are effectively tied, except for slightly lower dynamic degree, though qualitative results show no visible motion reduction. decoder finetuned on the same data with the same pixel losses reduces warping error only to 1.39 (Table 3 and Appendix B.1), so most of the gain comes from DWD rather than from the training data. 8-bit inference. Quantization degrades the baseline noticeably (warping error 1.52 to 1.69) but barely affects DWD (1.18 to 1.20), widening the warping error gap to 29% in Table 3. The other metrics follow the same pattern as under BF16. The DWD extension is thus robust to reducedprecision inference, and the quality gain over the decoder is larger in the deployment setting.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: DWD replaces the decoder with linear pixel head on the diffusion transformer, finetuning only the last few blocks and output heads. Across latent image and video generators, DWD preserves or improves pixel quality while removing the decoder entirely. On video, this visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering. On pixel diffusion models, separate DWD head recovers photorealistic texture that the denoising head oversmooths. The broader lesson is that final pixel prediction should be separated from intermediate denoising, so that pixel-space objectives can improve quality without interfering with the sampling trajectory. Limitations. The DWD quality gain shrinks when the decoder is already strong, as on FLUX.2. We have not proved that the linear head is sufficient for spatial patch sizes beyond 1616 pixels, where stronger head like DWD-conv may be needed. Also, we have not tuned the pixel losses per model, leaving potential room for improvement.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: This section complements Sec. 3 with the specifics of the DWD head, finetuning, inference, and evaluation, with per-model settings collected in Table 4. A.1 DWD HEAD Output format. The linear head maps each last-layer token to one pixel patch, and the patches are assembled into the image. Image models use 1616 patches. Wan uses 41616 spatiotemporal patches and separate 11616 head for the first latent frame, which covers single pixel frame in the Wan VAE. Following AsymFlow (Chen et al., 2026a), latent models and AnisoFlow-L/16T2I predict pixels in normalized Oklab color space (Ottosson, 2020), while the pixel quality losses are applied to the converted RGB values, matching the common autoencoder training recipe. The ImageNet pixel models predict RGB directly, matching their native output. Least-squares initialization. The head is initialized by linear regression from last-layer tokens to ground-truth pixel patches. We run the frozen pretrained model on 10k training images with timesteps drawn from ppix, the same distribution used for the pixel losses, and solve the normal equations for the weight and bias jointly. The same procedure produces the probes in Fig. 3, where the latent probe regresses from the denoised latent instead of the tokens. Convolutional head (DWD-conv). The DWD-conv ablation keeps the linear head and adds residual correction, following lightweight super-resolution networks (Shi et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2018; Ayazoglu, 2021): the nonlinear convolutions run at half resolution, final sub-pixel convolution (pixel shuffle) restores the full resolution, and the branch predicts residual over linear base prediction. It packs each 22 neighborhood of the linear pixel prediction into channels and refines this packed grid with convolutional branch. The last-layer tokens are projected through 128dimensional bottleneck and expanded into 32-channel spatial feature map, which is added to 11 projection of the packed pixels. Two residual blocks with 33 convolutions and SiLU activations predict the correction through zero-initialized output convolution, so the head starts as the linear head. For video, the convolutions operate on each frame independently. A.2 FINETUNING Table 4: DWD finetuning settings per model. is the number of finetuned blocks out of the total. Adv. start is the iteration at which the generator adversarial loss is switched on, after discriminator warmup. λ is the trajectory anchoring weight in Eq. The adversarial weight is set adaptively to match the gradient norm of the ℓ1 and LPIPS loss at the predicted pixels, following the gradient balancing of Esser et al. (2021) but measured at the pixels rather than at the last layers weights. The discriminator is trained for short warmup before the generator adversarial loss is switched on at the iteration listed in Table 4 (2.5k iterations of warmup for the ImageNet models, 1k for the others). Optimization. All runs use Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with learning rate 104, betas (0.9, 0.95), no weight decay, short linear warmup, and 5 learning rate for the DWD head. Weights are evaluated with the exponential moving average of Karras et al. (2024) (γ = 7), and Wan additionally caps the EMA momentum at 0.998. For FLUX.2 klein and Wan, the frozen blocks are quantized to FP8 during finetuning to reduce memory and speed up training. The frozen reference model is also quantized to FP8, while the trainable layers are trained in FP32 with BF16 mixed precision. The trainable layers therefore learn from slightly degraded FP8 reference, which works against DWD rather than favoring its 8-bit results. All main and qualitative results use BF16 inference. Training data. The ImageNet models are finetuned on the ImageNet training set at 256256. The text-to-image models are finetuned on the one-megapixel training data mix of AnisoFlow (Zirvi et al., 2026), consisting of TextAtlas (Wang et al., 2026a), RedCaps (Desai et al., 2021), and LAIONAesthetics (Schuhmann et al., 2022) images, with captions from i1 (Zeng et al., 2026) and AsymFlow (Chen et al., 2026a). FLUX.2 klein Base additionally trains on the same images downsampled to roughly 0.5 and 0.25 megapixels. The three tiers use per-iteration batch sizes of 128, 256, and 384 images and are sampled in the ratio 1:2:3. The video model is finetuned on clips from Vchitect T2V DataVerse (Fan et al., 2025) with the datasets captions. Clips are bucketed by resolution and length: 352640 with 81 or 33 frames (per-iteration batch sizes of 64 and 192 clips), 480832 with 81, 49, or 25 frames (32, 64, and 128 clips), and 7201280 with 33 or 17 frames (32 and 64 clips). Only source videos of at least 720p are used, so every training clip is downsampled from higher or equal source resolution rather than upscaled from low-bitrate video, which we found essential for sharp ground truth. A.3 INFERENCE Guidance and final step. Sampling follows each baselines default sampler and guidance, with one exception: the SiT-XL/2-REPA DWD extension uses guidance scale 2.3 on the interval [0, 0.56]. The final DWD step is evaluated once with the conditional input only, without classifier-free guidance pair. Since latent models favor larger final timestep (Fig. 4(a)), their final timestep is set manually as in Table 4, whereas the pixel models and the 4-step models use the last timestep of the baseline sampler. For Wan2.1 14B, the final timestep = 0.3 after shift of 7 corresponds to 0.058 before shifting. Its pixel loss skips timesteps below 0.02 before shifting, where Wans own predictions show strong color drift and detail degradation (common sampling grids do not use these timesteps either). 8-bit inference. The 8-bit setting quantizes all linear layers to FP8 weights and activations (W8A8) and replaces attention with the 8-bit SageAttention2 kernels (Zhang et al., 2025), for both the baseline and DWD. A.4 VIDEO EVALUATION Warping error (Lai et al., 2018) is computed for every pair of adjacent frames at native resolution: we estimate forward and backward optical flow with RAFT (Teed & Deng, 2020), warp the second frame onto the first, mask occlusions and motion boundaries by forward-backward consistency as in the released scorer of Lai et al. (2018), and average the squared RGB error over valid pixels following Xu et al. (2025). Errors are averaged over pairs within each video, then over videos. HPSv3 and HPSv2.1 are computed on five frames sampled uniformly from each video (one frame per second at 16 fps) and averaged. sections.title: B ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: B.1 DECODER-RETAINING BASELINE To separate decoder removal from the effect of the training data and pixel losses, we finetune the native Wan2.1 decoder on the same video data with the same ℓ1, LPIPS, and adversarial losses as DWD (Appendix A.2), using the same optimizer and EMA settings. The pretrained decoder is already well trained and its training loss stays flat, so we evaluate it after 2k iterations. In Table 3, the finetuned decoder reduces warping error only from 1.52 to 1.39, while DWD reduces it to 1.18, and the other metrics are effectively tied. Most of the DWD gain therefore comes from the method rather than from the training data. Finetuning the decoder is also not cheap: one decoder training iteration takes 24 s, about 2 slower than DWD iteration on Wan2.1 14B (12.5 s). B.2 FEW-STEP VIDEO GENERATION We apply DWD to the 4-step Wan2.1 T2V 1.3B model distilled with rCM (Zheng et al., 2026b), the example from Sec. 1. We finetune its last 8 of 30 blocks on the 352640 and 480832 tiers of the video data, and keep the samplers exact timesteps  (Table 4)  . The first 32.5k iterations use ptraj = [0.1, 0.94] and ppix = [0.02, 0.1], after which we switch to the ranges in Table 4 to match the final timestep of the 4-step sampler. In Table 5, DWD reduces warping error by 27% and improves temporal flickering. Note that the 1.3B model is an unfavorable setting for DWD. It is much smaller than Wan2.1 14B, and tuning only 8 blocks leaves limited learnable capacity. Self-distillation. With very few steps, the final step has to generate more content, so its pairing with real pixels becomes ambiguous, potentially making ℓ1 and perceptual losses less effective. We therefore also test self-distillation variant, which replaces the real pixels with target produced by chain: the reference models native final step, renoising to small timestep, and the pixel output of previously trained small-time DWD model. The results are shown in Table 5. In this experiment, the small-time DWD model is from the standard run after its first 32.5k iterations. The self-distillation DWD resumes from this checkpoint and continues to 40k iterations. This variant has nearly the same dynamic degree as the baseline (0.822 vs. 0.825) and still reduces warping error by 14%. Table 5: Few-step video generation on 4-step Wan2.1 T2V 1.3B (BF16). We compare the official AsymFlow and L2P models against their respective base models, FLUX.2 klein Base 9B (Black Forest Labs, 2025) and Z-Image Turbo (Z-Image Team et al., 2025). Both methods are substantially worse than their base models on the reported metrics  (Table 7)  , especially in text rendering  (Fig. 7)  . For AsymFlow, this is partly due to its sensitivity to the training data, which contains little text rendering, and partly due to the difficulty of adapting latent trajectory to pixel trajectory. In contrast, DWD matches the base model while preserving seed-level content. DWD is also much cheaper to train, requiring only about third of AsymFlows training cost (350 vs. 1100 H100 GPU hours) even with longer, saturated schedule (26k vs. 15k iterations). These models use decoder distillation variant, where the final steps ℓ1 and perceptual target becomes the output of the reference models native final step followed by the native decoder. Due to the extreme compression of the MiniMax-H3 autoencoder, each token covers 3232 spatial patch over maximum of 4 frames, so linear head would have up to 432323 = 12288 output dimensions, more than twice the DiTs hidden dimension of 5376. In addition, MiniMax-H3 is single-stream model, whose transformer weights are shared across text, visual, and audio tokens. Therefore, linear head has very limited capacity on these models, which benefit from lightweight refiner (e.g., the DWD-conv head in Appendix A.1). Please refer to our blog post (Chen et al., 2026b) for video results. These results are purely preliminary, since we have not yet determined the optimal refiner architecture.
